The morning light hit the windowsill differently today. I noticed it while making coffee, the way it caught the dust motes and made them look like something intentional, like tiny galaxies someone had arranged just for me. I stood there longer than I should have, watching them drift through that pale gold rectangle, and I thought about how much of life is just this—small performances of light and matter that we happen to witness, that would continue whether we watched or not.

I've been thinking about the word *witness* lately. Not the legal kind, not the religious kind exactly, though both carry weight. I mean the act of simply being present for something, the choice to not look away. My grandmother kept a garden for sixty years. She never called it meditation, never framed it as anything larger than "putting food on the table," but I watched her out there, kneeling among the tomatoes, and I understood that she was doing something else entirely. She was keeping company with growth itself. The slow, mostly invisible process of a seed becoming whatever it was meant to become. She was there for it. That mattered to someone, even if only to the plants.

We don't talk enough about the things that don't scale. The coffee with a friend where nothing important is said but something important happens anyway. The song heard at exactly the right wrong moment. The stranger who meets your eyes and doesn't immediately look away, that brief negotiation of recognition, two people agreeing for half a second that they are both real, both here, both equally improbable.

I used to want to be important in the way the world measures importance. Now I want to be present in the way a window is present. Just there, letting light through, offering a frame for whatever weather comes. Some days that feels like enough. Other days it feels like cowardice, like giving up. I haven't learned to tell the difference consistently.

The coffee got cold while I watched the dust. I drank it anyway. Lukewarm, slightly bitter, the way mornings go when you let them unfold without forcing direction. There was a whole day ahead, full of obligations I had agreed to, full of the small negotiations that make up a life. I would perform my competence, meet my deadlines, return my emails. But for those few minutes, I was just a body in a room, receiving light, and it was enough—it was more than enough—it was everything I didn't know I needed until it was offered without asking.
